Pauling (1931) proposed hybridization: the mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energy on the same atom to form the same number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals with the same energy and a definite shape.

The number of hybrids always equals the number of orbitals mixed, and hybrids overlap better than pure orbitals, so their bonds are stronger. One 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2p orbital, then the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to give four identical sp³ hybrids — which is why all four C–H bonds in methane are the same.

The type can be found easily from the steric number (bonds + lone pairs): 2 is sp, 3 is sp², 4 is sp³, 5 is sp³d and 6 is sp³d². It also says nothing about the shape or the strength of a bond — which is why the rest of this unit exists. The electrostatic force of attraction that holds together the oppositely charged ions produced by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.

The contact time is about 10⁻³ s: The reaction is so exothermic that once lit the gauze stays red hot without external heating. The contact time must be very short, because if the gases linger the nitric oxide decomposes back to nitrogen and oxygen.

The diaphragm cell does this with a porous barrier and a difference in liquid level. The cell is a steel tank divided by a diaphragm of asbestos (now usually a polymer-modified asbestos or a synthetic fibre) deposited on a perforated steel cathode.

The yield per pass is about 15%, but the overall yield is above 95% by recycling. The purified gases (ratio 1:3) are compressed, heated by heat exchangers, passed over the catalyst bed in the converter, then condensed and the ammonia is collected.

Expect one 8-mark question from this unit in almost every paper, plus stoichiometry numericals. Nitrogen is 78% of the air and utterly useless to most living things, because the N≡N triple bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is one of the strongest in chemistry.

One volume of ammonia to 8–10 volumes of air is passed through a glowing platinum–rhodium (90 : 10) gauze at 800 °C. The contact time is about 10⁻³ s: The reaction is so exothermic that once lit the gauze stays red hot without external heating.

Nitric acid: fertilisers (ammonium nitrate), explosives (TNT), dyes. Sulphuric acid: fertilisers (superphosphate), car batteries, detergents, metal cleaning and petroleum refining; its consumption is a rough indicator of industrial development.

It is cheap, a strong acid, a dehydrating agent, an oxidising agent at high concentration and a high-boiling liquid — so it turns up in fertilizer manufacture (its largest single use), detergents, dyes, paints, batteries and metal processing.

The product, blister copper, is about 98 per cent pure; escaping SO₂ makes the surface blistered. Blister copper is made the anode in an electrolytic cell of copper(II) sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid, with thin pure copper as the cathode.

The gas is cooled in a heat exchanger (raising steam for the rest of the plant) to about 50 °C and mixed with more air: This is an unusual reaction — it goes faster at lower temperature — so cooling helps both the rate and the equilibrium.

Saturated purified brine (about 25% NaCl) is fed continuously into the anode compartment and kept at a higher level than the liquid in the cathode compartment, so the flow of liquid through the diaphragm is always from anode to cathode.
